clue.text: Flying westwards, low in spirit

indicators.note: one word sits inside the other, placed within the outer word's letters

parts.note: zing is liveliness or pizzazz

indicators.note: in an across entry going westwards means travelling right to left, so the word is written backwards

parts.note: to low is what cattle do

explanation.surface: Someone is flying home westwards and feeling thoroughly depressed about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low in spirit' reads as a mood, but low is the cow's verb and spirit means zest or pizzazz; only the cow's word is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Zooming means moving very fast, and in the sense of an aircraft climbing steeply it is a kind of flight.

clue.text: Unknown university supported by productive finance hub

parts.note: algebra's unknowns are x, y and z
standard abbreviation for university
rich soil is fertile, productive

explanation.surface: An obscure college is bankrolled by a prosperous financial centre.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'supported by' puts the first pieces on top of the last.
explanation.definitionFit: The Swiss city is one of Europe's major banking and financial centres.

clue.text: Non-reciprocated love, fresh and ever poetic

parts.note: love is a zero score in tennis, shaped like O
fresh means new
ay (or aye) is a poetic word for ever, always

explanation.surface: Unrequited love, ever new, as a poet would put it.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-way feeling flows only from one side and is not returned by the other party.

clue.text: Misled to my failing in a shameful manner

indicators.note: a failing thing breaks down, so the letters before it fall apart and reform

parts.note: the ten letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone confesses that leading people astray was a shameful failing of theirs.
explanation.definitionFit: Immodest behaviour is indecent or shameless, so acting that way is acting without proper shame or decency.

clue.text: Entered bar, cycling

indicators.note: cycling moves letters round in a loop, taking some from the front to the back

parts.note: an ingot is a bar of metal such as gold

explanation.surface: Someone walked into a pub after riding their bike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub, but it is a bar of gold; move its first two letters to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To get in is a phrasal verb for gaining entry, so having got in is having gone inside.

clue.text: Tack round odd bits of thin fine fabric

indicators.note: the outer word goes round, enclosing the small selection

parts.note: to baste is to tack with long loose stitches

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters, first and third, are the only ones kept

parts.note: first and third letters, the odd-numbered ones

explanation.surface: A dressmaker's instruction: tack around scraps of a thin, delicate material.
explanation.definitionFit: Batiste is a sheer, lightweight cotton or linen cloth used for blouses and lingerie.

clue.text: Pompous manager almost frames business graduate with unlimited blame

indicators.note: a frame surrounds a picture, so the shortened word goes around the next one
almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a boss manages

indicators.note: with no limits means the outer boundary letters at each end are lost

parts.note: Master of Business Administration
to take stick is to take blame or criticism

explanation.surface: A self-important manager surrounds himself with an MBA and dishes out blame without limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take stick' is a British idiom for being blamed or criticised, which is how blame leads to the final piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Bombastic speech is high-flown and inflated, the language of a self-important, grandiloquent speaker.

clue.text: Error made by vacuous Teletubby and another

indicators.note: vacuous means empty, so the word is emptied of its insides, leaving its ends

parts.note: first and last letters
Po is another of the four Teletubbies, the small red one

explanation.surface: A mistake is blamed on a brainless children's TV character and one of its friends.
explanation.walkthrough: The Teletubbies are a British pre-school TV show with four characters: Tinky Winky, Dipsy, Laa-Laa and Po.
explanation.definitionFit: A typo is a typing slip, a small printed or keyboard mistake.

clue.text: Hurry set point after a couple of upsets?

indicators.note: a pair of upsets leaves things overturned and jumbled, so the preceding letters are reordered

parts.note: the eight letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A tennis player races to reach set point after two shock results.
explanation.walkthrough: The tennis scene makes 'upsets' sound like surprise defeats; here they mean letters knocked out of order.
explanation.definitionFit: Step on it is an idiom from pressing the accelerator pedal, telling a driver to go faster.

clue.text: Denounce cost of administration?

parts.note: short for executive, the administration
a rate is a charge or price

explanation.surface: Someone condemns the cost of running an organisation's administration.
explanation.walkthrough: Split 4,4 the answer reads as an executive rate, the cost of administration, read in that order.
explanation.definitionFit: To execrate is to curse or loudly condemn something as detestable.

clue.text: What about cutting Hebridean island's rhubarb?

indicators.note: cutting into something means going inside it

parts.note: Rum is an island in the Inner Hebrides, off western Scotland

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the short word is read backwards

parts.note: eh? is a request to repeat: what?

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a rhubarb crop is being cut on a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rhubarb' looks like nonsense talk, but it is the plant; Rheum is its botanical genus.
explanation.definitionFit: Rheum is the scientific genus name for the rhubarb plants, also used in Chambers for the plant itself.

clue.text: Retrospectively give out prize case for carriage clock?

indicators.note: looking back in time suggests reading backwards from the end

parts.note: to emit is to give out
Chambers gives pie as an informal word for a prize or spoil

indicators.note: a case is an outer covering, so only the outside letters are taken

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: Handing out a prize in its case: an old-fashioned carriage clock for a retiring employee.
explanation.walkthrough: Only 'give out' is reversed; the rest follows in order. 'Carriage' looks like part of the definition but supplies its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A clock is a timekeeping device, and the question mark flags the wordplay leaning on the phrase carriage clock.

clue.text: Against drinking vigorous — no, old — wine

indicators.note: a drinker takes something inside, so one word swallows the other

parts.note: pros and cons: con means against
hard as in a hard, vigorous effort
nay is an archaic word for no

explanation.surface: A temperance campaigner, firmly opposed to heavy drinking, refuses wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Chardonnay is a white grape variety and the dry white wine made from it.

clue.text: Square that's right here …

parts.note: surface reading: someone points to a square on a map, saying it is right here
setter's reading: a square number that is printed right here, at the far right of the clue in the enumeration

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the number in brackets at the right of this very clue; the ellipsis carries on into the next clue's surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Two times two gives this number, which makes it a perfect square in arithmetic.

clue.text: C'est la guerre, say some firing indiscriminately

indicators.note: firing without discrimination scatters shots at random, so the letters land in random order

parts.note: the ten letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Following the previous clue: a soldier shrugs 'that's war' as shots are fired at random.
explanation.definitionFit: A French phrase used in English is a borrowed expression from another language, and 'say' marks it as one example.

clue.text: Who might have condemned liaisons with Tito?

definitions.text: Who might have condemned liaisons with Tito?

indicators.note: something condemned is wrecked or ruined, so the letters are broken up and remade

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written: the Yugoslav leader

explanation.surface: Who would have objected to links with Marshal Tito's Yugoslavia during the Cold War?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and the wordplay at once: an anagram of LIAISONS + TITO.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone favouring a policy of staying apart from foreign alliances would oppose forming ties with any foreign leader.

clue.text: See female smile in opera

parts.note: lo! means look, see
a hen is a female bird
a grin is a broad smile

explanation.surface: Watch a woman smiling during an opera performance.
explanation.definitionFit: Lohengrin is Wagner's romantic opera about the swan knight, first staged in 1850.

clue.text: Olympiads, not one playing devotional songs

indicators.note: playing means performing freely, so the letters are moved around
one is I, and 'not' takes it away from the word

parts.note: taken as written: the sporting festivals

explanation.surface: Hymns are being played at the Olympics, though none by a soloist.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one I from OLYMPIADS, then rearrange the remaining eight.
explanation.definitionFit: Psalmody is the singing of psalms, and by extension the collected psalms or hymns themselves.

clue.text: Black and gold invention buried in heart of pseudo Hampshire village

indicators.note: something buried lies inside the ground, so these go within the next piece

parts.note: pencil grading abbreviation for black

indicators.note: the heart is the middle, so the central letters are kept

parts.note: the two central letters
chemical symbol for gold
a lie is a made-up story

explanation.surface: A fake treasure story is found deep in a sham English village.
explanation.walkthrough: Hampshire is a county on England's south coast; the village, near the New Forest, is pronounced 'BEW-lee'.
explanation.definitionFit: Beaulieu is a village in the New Forest, Hampshire, home to the National Motor Museum.

clue.text: Dazed groups of agents with leader splitting hamstring in drop

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the outer word

parts.note: to shed is to drop or cast off

indicators.note: to split is to leave, so the first letter departs from that word

parts.note: cells are small groups of spies or terrorists
to hock is to hamstring, disabling by cutting the leg tendon

explanation.surface: A spy ring's chief is left reeling after his hamstring tears in a fall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Splitting' looks like a tear in the muscle, but it means leaving: the cells lose their first letter. The word for drop is itself split open to hold the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Shell-shocked describes someone stunned and bewildered, originally from soldiers traumatised by bombardment.

clue.text: Violet-blue mythical monster decapitated

indicators.note: losing the head means the first letter is removed

parts.note: the windigo is a man-eating creature of Algonquian folklore

explanation.surface: A legendary beast, beheaded, is bruised a purplish blue.
explanation.definitionFit: Indigo is the deep colour between blue and violet in the rainbow spectrum.

clue.text: One month patrolling Bronze Sector

indicators.note: a patrol goes all around an area, so one word surrounds the next

parts.note: abbreviation for October, one month
a tan is a bronzed skin colour

explanation.surface: For a month, someone patrols the Bronze Sector, like a guard on a military zone.
explanation.definitionFit: An octant is an eighth of a circle, a sector bounded by two radii at 45 degrees.

clue.text: Praise twin from the east

indicators.note: in an across entry, starting at the east means reading right to left

parts.note: twin and dual both mean double

explanation.surface: Someone sings the praises of a twin who has come from the East.
explanation.definitionFit: To laud is to praise highly, extol or glorify.

clue.text: Outside Germany, dreadful ignorance about male hormones

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase: relating to male hormones

indicators.note: the jumbled word sits outside, wrapping round the abbreviation
dreadful means very bad, so the letters are in a terrible mess

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
D is the international vehicle code for Germany (Deutschland)

explanation.surface: A complaint that outside Germany there is shocking ignorance concerning testosterone.
explanation.definitionFit: Androgenic means relating to or producing androgens, the hormones that develop masculine characteristics.

clue.text: Going over lump, drive back

indicators.note: in a down entry, going over means flipping upside down

parts.note: a tuber is a swollen lump on a root, like a potato

explanation.surface: A car hits a bump in the road and the driver reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: Rebut can mean to repel or force back an attack, as well as to refute an argument.

clue.text: Picked up top dog

indicators.note: picked up as in heard, caught by ear on a radio

parts.note: a peak is a summit, the top

explanation.surface: Someone lifts up the best dog at a show.
explanation.definitionFit: A peke is short for Pekingese, a small long-haired toy breed from China.

clue.text: Green poet ill, old, withdrawn

indicators.note: something withdrawn is drawn back, so the string is read backwards

parts.note: a bard is a poet
ill as in harm, wickedness
standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: An elderly, sickly poet has withdrawn from society, inexperienced in the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Green' looks like an adjective meaning naive, but it is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Olive drab is the dull greyish-green shade used for military uniforms.

clue.text: Business rival regularly checks clubbing-holiday Mecca?

indicators.note: to check is to hold back or restrain, so these letters hold the other piece
at regular intervals, every other letter is chosen

parts.note: second and fourth letters
biz is slang for business, as in showbiz

explanation.surface: A business competitor keeps an eye on a party resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Business' looks like the word to take letters from regularly, but the regular letters come from rival and they surround a slang word for business.
explanation.definitionFit: The Balearic island is world-famous for its nightclubs and summer dance-music tourism.

clue.text: I agree to challenge Telegraph's English in that sometime

indicators.note: the first pieces go inside the outer word

parts.note: yon is a once-common word for that, now archaic
the clue appears in the Telegraph, so the paper's own is 'our'
standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A writer accepts a challenge to publish the paper's English column some time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sometime' means formerly, marking yon as an old word.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a colloquial way of accepting a bet or dare, meaning the deal is agreed.

clue.text: Herb caught and bowled, perhaps causing stoppage in play

indicators.note: caught here means heard, picked up by the ear

parts.note: thyme is a kitchen herb
being bowled is one way a batsman is out in cricket

explanation.surface: A cricketer named Herb is dismissed caught and bowled, halting the game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught and bowled' is a single cricket dismissal, but the clue splits it: caught means heard.
explanation.definitionFit: A time-out is a short break called during a game, halting the action.
